steps.title: Friendly or polite you
steps.how_to: How to greet and ask after someone with tu or Lei.
steps.intro: In this step you'll learn two ways to say 'how are you?': one for friends and one for shopkeepers and older people. You'll use them every time you greet someone here.
steps.notice: With a friend you say 'come stai' and 'e tu'. With a shopkeeper or an older person you say 'come sta' and 'e Lei'. When you're unsure, use Lei until they offer tu.

ask.said: Cosa chiedi a un amico quando lo vedi?
ask.en: What do you ask a friend when you see him?

ask.said: Un amico ti dice: «Ciao, come stai?» Cosa rispondi?
ask.en: A friend says to you: 'Hi, how are you?' What do you answer?

ask.said: Una signora anziana ti dice: «Come sta?» Cosa rispondi?
ask.en: An older lady says to you: 'How are you?' What do you answer?

mission.goal: Greet the barista politely and ask how they are.

steps.title: Say how you are
steps.how_to: How to say how you are with sto.
steps.intro: Now you'll be able to answer 'how are you?' the way people here do. You'll say it every time a shopkeeper or neighbour asks.
steps.notice: The question and the answer use the same word: sta or stai when you ask, sto when you answer. To say you're well, say 'Sto bene'.

ask.said: Come stai?
ask.en: How are you?

ask.said: Un negoziante ti dice: «Come sta?» Cosa rispondi?
ask.en: A shopkeeper says to you: 'How are you?' What do you answer?

ask.said: Come stai oggi? Chiedi anche a me.
ask.en: How are you today? Ask me too.

mission.goal: Say you're well and ask the shopkeeper back.

steps.title: Greet by time of day
steps.how_to: How to choose between buongiorno, buonasera and buonanotte.
steps.intro: You'll learn which hello fits the hour, so you greet people right whether it's morning or evening. You'll use it each time you walk into a bar, shop or restaurant.
steps.notice: Buongiorno is for the morning and early afternoon, and buonasera takes over for the rest of the day, even at 9 p.m. Buonanotte is the one you say when someone is going to bed.
steps.context: Buonasera starts surprisingly early, around 3 or 4 p.m.

ask.said: Come saluti il barista alle dieci di mattina?
ask.en: How do you greet the barista at ten in the morning?

ask.said: Come saluti una signora in negozio alle cinque?
ask.en: How do you greet a lady in a shop at five?

ask.said: Cosa dici a un vicino prima di andare a letto?
ask.en: What do you say to a neighbour before going to bed?

mission.goal: Greet the waiter with the right hello for the evening.

steps.title: Saying you didn't understand
steps.how_to: How to say that you didn't understand or don't speak much Italian.
steps.intro: Here is the phrase you'll use most in your first weeks. You'll say it at a counter, in a shop or in the piazza whenever someone speaks too fast.
steps.notice: In every line, non sits right in front of the verb. Nothing else is needed, so you just say non ho capito.
steps.context: Most people are pleased you're trying.

ask.said: Hai capito?
ask.en: Did you understand?

ask.said: Parli bene l'italiano?
ask.en: Do you speak Italian well?

answer.en: No, I don't speak Italian well.

ask.said: Cosa dici quando la gente parla troppo veloce?
ask.en: What do you say when people speak too fast?

mission.goal: Tell the shopkeeper you didn't understand.

steps.title: Asking someone to repeat
steps.how_to: How to politely ask someone to repeat or speak more slowly.
steps.intro: With these phrases you can ask people to say it again, or slower. You'll use them when you miss a price or an answer.

examples.en: Could you repeat that? (to a friend)
Could you say it in English?

steps.notice: Può comes first, then the basic form of the verb straight after it, with no little word between them. With a friend, use puoi instead of può.
steps.context: Asking someone to go more slowly with più piano, per favore is normal and expected.

ask.said: Come chiedi a un amico di ripetere?
ask.en: How do you ask a friend to repeat?

ask.said: Non hai sentito il prezzo. Cosa chiedi al cassiere?
ask.en: You didn't catch the price. What do you ask the cashier?

ask.said: Il barista parla veloce. Cosa gli chiedi?
ask.en: The barista speaks fast. What do you ask him?

answer.said: Può parlare più piano, per favore?
answer.en: Could you speak more slowly, please?

mission.goal: Ask the shopkeeper to repeat the price.

steps.title: Saying you got it
steps.how_to: How to say you understood, or didn't, about what was just said.
steps.intro: You can use these two short phrases right away. You'll say them when someone has just spoken to you and you want to show whether it clicked.
steps.notice: Ho capito means you got it, and non ho capito means you didn't. For something someone has just said, these are the phrases to use. To ask someone else, say Ha capito?, or Hai capito? to a friend.

ask.said: Il cassiere ripete il prezzo. Hai capito?
ask.en: The cashier repeats the price. Did you understand?

ask.said: Cosa dici quando capisci finalmente?
ask.en: What do you say when you finally understand?

ask.said: Il farmacista parla veloce. Hai capito?
ask.en: The pharmacist speaks fast. Did you understand?

mission.goal: Say you got it after someone repeats something.

steps.title: Asking about words
steps.how_to: How to ask what a word means, how to say it, or how to spell it.
steps.intro: These three questions help you learn new words on the spot. You'll use them when you meet a word you don't know at a counter or in a shop.

examples.en: How do you say “receipt” in Italian?

steps.notice: Learn these as ready-made questions: come si dice, come si scrive, cosa vuol dire. Say them just like this and add the word you're asking about.
steps.context: To say “Sorry?” Italians say Come? or Scusi?

ask.said: Non conosci una parola. Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: You don't know a word. What do you ask?

ask.said: Non sai dire una parola in italiano. Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: You can't say a word in Italian. What do you ask?

answer.en: How do you say “receipt” in Italian?

ask.said: Vuoi scrivere una parola nuova. Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: You want to write a new word. What do you ask?

mission.goal: Ask how to say a word in Italian.

say.en: How do you say “receipt” in Italian?

steps.title: Saying I am, you are
steps.how_to: How to say who you are and ask someone else with sono, sei and è.
steps.intro: Now you can say who you are and ask a neighbour the same. You'll use it the moment someone stops you at your building door.
steps.notice: Sono is I am, sei is you are with a friend, and è is you are with Lei. The verb already says who, so just start with 'Sono'.

ask.said: Sei qui in vacanza?
ask.en: Are you here on holiday?

answer.said: No, sono qui per imparare l'italiano.
answer.en: No, I'm here to learn Italian.

ask.said: Di dove sei?
ask.en: Where are you from?

ask.said: Sei in pensione?
ask.en: Are you retired?

mission.goal: Tell a neighbour you're American.

steps.title: Telling people your name
steps.how_to: How to give your name and ask for theirs.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say your name and ask for someone else's. It's the first thing you do when you meet a neighbour or a classmate.

examples.said: Piacere! E Lei, come si chiama?
examples.en: Nice to meet you! And what's your name?
Nice to meet you, I'm Rosa.

steps.notice: Mi chiamo gives your name. To ask, start with come: 'Come si chiama?' with Lei, 'Come ti chiami?' with a friend. Then just add the name after mi chiamo.

ask.said: Come ti chiami?
ask.en: What's your name?

ask.said: E tu, come ti chiami?
ask.en: And what's your name?

answer.en: My name's …. Nice to meet you!

ask.said: Ti chiami Marco?
ask.en: Is your name Marco?

mission.goal: Give your name and ask a neighbour's name.

say.said: Mi chiamo …. E Lei, come si chiama?
say.en: My name's …. And what's your name?

steps.title: Saying where you live
steps.how_to: How to say where you live and ask someone else.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say that you live here and ask a neighbour where they live. Use it when someone asks if you're on holiday.
steps.notice: Abito is I live. Ask a friend 'Dove abiti?' and ask someone you address as Lei 'Dove abita?'. The ending changes, so listen to it.
steps.context: When you say you live here, people start treating you as a neighbour.

ask.said: Sei qui in vacanza?
ask.en: Are you here on holiday?

ask.said: Abiti qui?
ask.en: Do you live here?

ask.said: Dove abiti?
ask.en: Where do you live?

mission.goal: Tell a neighbour you live here.

steps.title: Saying your nationality
steps.how_to: How to say you're American or English, as a man or a woman.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say what nationality you are. People here ask it early, so it's handy to have ready.

examples.en: I'm English. (a man or a woman)

steps.notice: A woman changes americano to americana. Words ending in -e, like inglese, stay the same for everyone.

ask.said: Sei americano?
ask.en: Are you American?

ask.said: Sei inglese?
ask.en: Are you English?

ask.said: Sei italiana?
ask.en: Are you Italian?

mission.goal: Say your nationality to a neighbour.

steps.title: Saying where you're from
steps.how_to: How to say your city, where you live and your country.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say which city you come from, where you live and in which country. People here often ask where you're from.
steps.notice: Use sono di plus your city for where you're from. Use abito a plus a city, and abito in plus a country.
steps.context: 'Di dove sei?' is one of the first things Italians ask, because where you come from matters a lot here.

ask.said: Di dove sei?
ask.en: Where are you from?

ask.said: Dove abiti?
ask.en: Where do you live?

ask.said: In quale paese abiti?
ask.en: In which country do you live?

mission.goal: Tell a neighbour which city you're from.

steps.title: Saying how long you've been here
steps.how_to: How to say how long you've been in Italy.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say how long you've been here and why you came. It's a good answer when a neighbour is curious about you.

examples.en: And are you here on holiday?

examples.said: Sono in Italia da tre settimane.
examples.en: I've been in Italy for three weeks.
I've been here for three weeks.
I've been studying Italian for a month.

steps.notice: Italian says it in the present: sono, then da and the time. The time is still going, so it stays in the present.

ask.said: Da quanto tempo sei in Italia?
ask.en: How long have you been in Italy?

answer.en: I've been in Italy for … weeks.

ask.said: Da quanto tempo abiti qui?
ask.en: How long have you lived here?

ask.said: Da quanto tempo studi l'italiano?
ask.en: How long have you been studying Italian?

answer.en: I've been studying Italian for a month.

mission.goal: Tell a neighbour how long you've been in Italy.

say.said: Sono in Italia da tre settimane.
say.en: I've been in Italy for three weeks.

steps.title: Saying a or an
steps.how_to: How to say 'a' or 'an' before a drink or a snack.
steps.intro: Every drink and snack needs a little word in front, like 'a coffee' or 'a spritz'. You'll use it every time you order at the bar.
steps.notice: Most words take un, like un caffè. Spritz takes uno, spremuta takes una, and aranciata takes un' with an apostrophe. Learn each word together with its little word.

ask.said: Cosa prendi la mattina al bar?
ask.en: What do you have in the morning at the bar?

ask.said: E per l'aperitivo, cosa prendi?
ask.en: And for an aperitivo, what do you have?

ask.said: Hai sete. Cosa chiedi al barista?
ask.en: You're thirsty. What do you ask the barista for?

mission.goal: Order a spritz with the right word for 'a'.

steps.title: Ordering more than one
steps.how_to: How to order two of the same drink or snack.
steps.intro: When you're with a friend, you'll want to order two of something. Here is how to say it at the bar.

examples.said: Allora, due caffè. Al banco o al tavolo?
examples.en: So, two coffees. At the counter or at a table?

steps.notice: Words ending in -o or -a change their last letter: cappuccino becomes cappuccini, and spremuta becomes spremute. Words ending in an accent, like caffè and tè, stay just the same: due caffè.
steps.context: Standing at the banco costs less than sitting at a table.

ask.said: Sei al bar con un amico. Cosa chiedi da mangiare?
ask.en: You're at the bar with a friend. What do you ask for to eat?

ask.said: Di mattina, cosa chiedi da bere per voi due?
ask.en: In the morning, what do you ask for to drink for the two of you?

ask.said: E dopo pranzo, cosa chiedi per voi due?
ask.en: And after lunch, what do you ask for the two of you?

mission.goal: Order two coffees for you and a friend.

steps.title: Asking politely with vorrei
steps.how_to: How to ask politely for anything with vorrei.
steps.intro: Vorrei means 'I'd like', and it's the polite way to ask for something. You can use it at the bar, the market or anywhere you order.

examples.en: Yes? What can I get you?
I'd like a fresh orange juice.

examples.said: Vorrei un bicchiere d'acqua, per favore.
examples.en: I'd like a glass of water, please.

examples.said: Per me un cappuccino e un cornetto.
examples.en: A cappuccino and a croissant for me.

steps.notice: Vorrei plus the item is a polite way to ask for anything, and you can use it just as it is. Per me plus the item is another friendly way to order.
steps.context: Italians have cappuccino in the morning, so it's a breakfast order.

ask.said: Sei al bar la mattina. Cosa ordini da bere?
ask.en: You're at the bar in the morning. What do you order to drink?

ask.said: Vuoi qualcosa di fresco da bere. Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: You want something fresh to drink. What do you ask for?

answer.en: I'd like a fresh orange juice.

ask.said: Al barista chiedi anche dell'acqua. Come dici?
ask.en: You also ask the barista for water. What do you say?

answer.said: Vorrei un bicchiere d'acqua, per favore.
answer.en: I'd like a glass of water, please.

mission.goal: Ask politely for a fresh orange juice.

say.said: Vorrei una spremuta d'arancia, per favore.
say.en: I'd like a fresh orange juice, please.

steps.title: Saying what you'll have
steps.how_to: How to say what you'll have and ask what others are having.
steps.intro: In Italian you 'take' food and drink, so the verb is prendere. You'll use it to say what you're having and to ask a friend or a stranger the same.
steps.notice: Prendo means 'I'll have', and you add the item after it. Cosa prendi? is for a friend, and Cosa prende? is for someone you speak to politely.

ask.said: Sei al bar con un amico. Cosa prendi?
ask.en: You're at the bar with a friend. What are you having?

ask.said: Il tuo amico ordina un caffè. Tu prendi la stessa cosa. Cosa dici?
ask.en: Your friend orders a coffee. You have the same. What do you say?

ask.said: Come chiedi a un amico cosa vuole ordinare?
ask.en: How do you ask a friend what they want to order?

mission.goal: Say what you'll have at the counter.

steps.title: Numbers up to thousands
steps.how_to: How to say and understand numbers, from twenty up to two thousand.
steps.intro: Now you'll be able to understand a price when the cashier says it, and say numbers back. You'll hear them at every till, stall and ticket window.
steps.notice: Numbers are built just like in English: venti and tre make ventitré, with an accent. Before uno and otto the tens lose their last vowel: ventuno, ventotto, trentuno. After cento comes mille, and two thousand is duemila.

ask.said: Come dici 31 euro in italiano?
ask.en: How do you say 31 euros in Italian?

ask.said: Come dici 23 euro in italiano?
ask.en: How do you say 23 euros in Italian?

ask.said: Come dici 2.000 in italiano?
ask.en: How do you say 2,000 in Italian?

mission.goal: Say the price back to the cashier to check it.

steps.title: Saying euros and cents
steps.how_to: How to say a price in euros, with or without the cents.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say and understand prices like two euros seventy. You'll use it whenever you pay or check a total.
steps.notice: The word euro stays the same for one or many: un euro, due euro. The number after e is the cents, and people often leave the word out: quattro e cinquanta means 4.50. If a price sounds odd, just ask again.

ask.said: Come dici 1 euro in italiano?
ask.en: How do you say 1 euro in Italian?

ask.said: Come dici 3,20 euro in italiano?
ask.en: How do you say 3.20 euros in Italian?

ask.said: Come dici 4,50 euro in italiano?
ask.en: How do you say 4.50 euros in Italian?

mission.goal: Ask the total at the till after you order.

steps.title: Asking how much
steps.how_to: How to ask the price of one thing or of several things.
steps.intro: You'll be able to ask what something costs, whether it's one item or a few. You'll use it at the market, in shops and at the newsstand.
steps.notice: One thing is costa, several things are costano, and the thing you're asking about comes after. If you just point, say Quanto costa? with nothing before it.

ask.said: Come chiedi il prezzo del pane?
ask.en: How do you ask the price of the bread?

ask.said: Al giornalaio, come chiedi il prezzo del giornale?
ask.en: At the newsstand, how do you ask the price of the newspaper?

ask.said: Come chiedi il prezzo delle pesche?
ask.en: How do you ask the price of the peaches?

mission.goal: Ask the price of something at a stall.

steps.title: Paying by card or cash
steps.how_to: How to ask if you can pay by card or cash.
steps.intro: You'll be able to ask to pay the way you like, and answer when the cashier asks for change. You'll use it at every till.

examples.en: Sorry, I haven't got any change.

steps.notice: Posso means can I, and the next word keeps its basic form: posso pagare. You can also just say Pago in contanti, and hand over the money with Ecco a Lei.
steps.context: Cashiers at small shops and market stalls often ask Ha moneta? to avoid breaking a big note.

ask.said: Come chiedi se puoi pagare con la carta?
ask.en: How do you ask if you can pay by card?

ask.said: Come chiedi se puoi pagare in contanti?
ask.en: How do you ask if you can pay cash?

ask.said: Il cassiere chiede: Ha moneta? Tu non hai spiccioli. Cosa rispondi?
ask.en: The cashier asks if you have change. You have none. What do you answer?

answer.en: Sorry, I haven't got any change.

mission.goal: Ask to pay by card at the till.
